overview.title: 📖 Overview: Twin Firstborns, Priestly Gifts, and a New Mishna
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 18a–18b
overview.hebrewSource: שְׁתֵּי רְחֵילָיו שֶׁלֹּא בִּיכְּרוּ וְיָלְדוּ שְׁנֵי זְכָרִים — שְׁנֵיהֶם לַכֹּהֵן
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by closing the question left hanging on 17b: does a baraita about a corpse found equidistant between two towns prove that human measurements can be exact? After testing and rejecting several readings, the Gemara concludes the Rabbis hold that even matters in human hands cannot coincide with true precision. It then returns to the twin-firstborn mishna, with Rabbi Yoḥanan clarifying that Rabbi Akiva's 'they assess between them' actually means the priest takes the leaner animal, and a dense set of rulings works out exactly when the owner must give the priest gifts of the priesthood from the uncertain second lamb. Two parables — sheep deposited with a shared shepherd versus with a private homeowner — explain why Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva disagree only in one specific scenario. The daf closes with a new mishna cataloguing every combination of two ewes giving birth together.

slides.title: ⚖️ אפשר לצמצם: The Rabbis' Final Position
slides.subtitle: Continuing from 17b: can two towns be truly equidistant from a corpse?

steps.content: 1️⃣ Suggestion: the baraita's first tanna (no heifer brought at all) disputes Rabbi Eliezer (two heifers brought) over whether precise measurement is possible
2️⃣ Rejected: if the first tanna truly held precision impossible, he should still bring one heifer in partnership — not refuse to bring any!
3️⃣ Real dispute: both tannaim agree precision is possible; they disagree only whether the singular 'קְרוֹבָה' (nearest) excludes multiple equally-near towns
4️⃣ So what do the actual Rabbis (who oppose Rabbi Eliezer) hold? A baraita reports: they rule to bring one heifer in partnership

5️⃣ Conclusion: had they held precision possible with 'קרובה' including multiple, they'd bring two; had they excluded multiple, they'd bring none. Bringing exactly one proves they hold precision impossible even in human hands

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: This settles the question raised on 17b about whether two events — including simultaneous births — can ever truly coincide.

slides.title: 🐑 'They Assess Between Them' — What Did Rabbi Akiva Mean?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba questions Rabbi Yoḥanan's reading

lines.speaker: Mishna
lines.text: Rabbi Tarfon: the priest chooses the better of the two lambs — presumed that the healthier one emerged first.

lines.speaker: R' Yoḥanan
lines.text: But Rabbi Akiva's 'they assess [מְשַׁמְּנִין] between them' actually means the priest takes the leaner of the two.

lines.speaker: R' Ḥiyya b. Abba
lines.text: Didn't we learn 'they assess the value between them' — meaning they divide the value?

lines.speaker: R' Yoḥanan
lines.text: While you were eating dates in Babylonia, we in Eretz Yisrael explained it from the mishna's latter clause.

lines.speaker: Proof
lines.text: If one lamb dies: Rabbi Tarfon says divide the survivor; Rabbi Akiva says the owner keeps it (burden of proof on the claimant). If 'assess' meant splitting value, that case should split too — it doesn't!

lines.speaker: Conclusion
lines.text: Rather, 'מְשַׁמְּנִין' means the extra fat [שׁוּמָּן] of the better lamb is disputed: the owner tells the priest, 'bring proof it is the firstborn, and take it.'

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: Rabbi Akiva's ruling gives the leaner lamb outright to the priest, while the better one stays with the owner unless the priest can prove his claim.

slides.title: 🎁 Priestly Gifts on the Uncertain Second Lamb
slides.subtitle: When must the owner give the foreleg, jaw, and maw from the grazing lamb he eventually slaughters?
rows: Rabbi Meir
Obligates the gifts
The priest 'comes at him from two sides': if it is the firstborn, it's entirely his; if not, at least give the gifts
Rabbi Yosei
Exempts — only where a replacement lamb is already in the priest's possession
The Sages treat one who never actually acquired it as though he did — the priest 'sold' it back to the owner
Rabbi Elazar's caveat
Everyone agrees the owner is obligated
When no replacement ever reached the priest at all (e.g. a male and female twin) — Rabbi Yosei's reasoning doesn't apply
Rav Pappa's caveat
Everyone agrees the owner is exempt
For an animal of uncertain tithe status — even Rabbi Meir agrees, since there the priest never 'comes at him from two sides'

callout.label: Key phrase:
callout.text: חֲלִיפִין בְּיַד כֹּהֵן — 'a replacement in the priest's possession' — is the hinge Rabbi Yosei's entire exemption turns on.

slides.title: 🤝 Two Parables Explain Tarfon and Akiva
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Ḥiyya: their real dispute is narrower than it first appears

boxes.title: Two Depositors, One Shepherd
items: Two people each deposit a sheep with a shepherd; one animal dies, unclear whose
Everyone agrees: the shepherd places the survivor between them and withdraws — they divide its value
Maps to Rabbi Tarfon's case: the owner's courtyard is partly transferred to the priest, since he wants the mitzva performed

boxes.title: One Depositor, a Homeowner
items: One person deposits a sheep with a homeowner who has flocks of his own; unclear whose animal died
Everyone agrees: the burden of proof rests on the claimant — the depositor
Maps to Rabbi Akiva's case: the owner never transfers courtyard rights, since it could cost him money

boxes.title: Where They Truly Disagree
items: Only about a birth in the owner's own courtyard, with a priest as the usual recipient
Rabbi Tarfon: the owner effectively 'deposits' with the priest by wanting the mitzva done there
Rabbi Akiva: since it could cost the owner, he transfers nothing — it stays purely his courtyard

callout.label: Retraction:
callout.text: Rabbi Ami reports that Rabbi Tarfon actually retracted his 'priest chooses the better one' ruling and holds, like the parable, that they always divide the value — the mishna's text was simply never updated.

slides.title: 📋 Two Ewes Give Birth: The New Mishna's Cases
slides.subtitle: Every combination of two never-yet-given-birth ewes bearing together
rows: Both ewes bear males
Both lambs go to the priest — each is its own mother's firstborn
One bears a male, one a female
The male goes to the priest
Two males and one female (three offspring)
One male kept by owner, one given to priest — subject to the Tarfon/Akiva dispute
Two females and a male, or two males and two females
The priest gets nothing — perhaps both ewes bore females first
One ewe had given birth before, one had not, and both bear males
One to owner, one to priest — same Tarfon/Akiva dispute and Rabbi Yosei's gifts exemption apply

callout.label: Gemara's question:
callout.text: Why does the mishna repeat the Tarfon/Akiva dispute across three near-identical cases? Because in each, one might have thought Rabbi Akiva would concede to Rabbi Tarfon that the presumed-better lamb came from a particular mother.

summary.principle: Precise coincidence is impossible even in human hands, and every uncertain-firstborn ruling — from Rabbi Akiva's 'leaner lamb' to the priestly gifts — is built on how that uncertainty is allocated between owner and priest.

flowSteps.content: 📋 New mishna: every combination of two ewes' simultaneous births and who gets which lamb
🎓 Key Principle: Uncertainty about a firstborn is resolved not by guessing which animal is holier, but by tracking who legally holds — or never held — the disputed animal

quiz.q: What did the Gemara conclude about the Rabbis' position on whether two matters in human hands can coincide precisely, based on the eglah arufah baraita?
o: They hold it is always possible
They hold it is impossible, even in human hands
They never addressed the question
They hold it depends on the case
quiz.e: Since the Rabbis rule to bring exactly one heifer in partnership — not two (if precision were possible) and not zero (if 'kerova' excluded multiple towns) — the Gemara concludes they hold precise coincidence is impossible even for human measurement.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yoḥanan, what does Rabbi Akiva's ruling 'they assess (מְשַׁמְּנִין) between them' actually mean?
o: The priest and owner divide the value of both lambs equally
The priest automatically receives the fatter lamb
The priest takes the leaner lamb, while the fat one's status is disputed and requires proof
The owner keeps both lambs
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan explains that the leaner lamb goes to the priest outright, while the extra fat (שׁוּמָּן) of the better lamb remains disputed — the owner tells the priest to bring proof it is the firstborn before taking it.

quiz.q: What is Rabbi Meir's reasoning for obligating the owner to give priestly gifts from the uncertain second lamb?
o: The gifts must never be forgotten as a category
The priest 'comes at him from two sides' — if it's the firstborn it's all his, if not, he's still owed the gifts
The lamb is definitely not a firstborn
Rabbi Yosei agrees with him in every case
quiz.e: Rabbi Meir's stated reasoning (per Rabbi Yoḥanan) is that the priest has a double claim on the second lamb — full ownership if it is the firstborn, or at least the gifts if it is not — so the owner must give the gifts regardless.

quiz.q: Why does Rabbi Yosei exempt the owner from giving gifts when a replacement lamb is already in the priest's possession?
o: Because gifts are never required from firstborns
Because the Sages treat one who never actually acquired the animal as though he had acquired and then sold it back
Because Rabbi Yosei rejects the concept of priestly gifts entirely
Because the lamb in question is always blemished
quiz.e: Rava explains Rabbi Yosei's reasoning: the Sages render one who did not truly acquire the animal (the priest, regarding the second lamb) as though he did acquire it and then sold it back to the owner in its blemished state — so the owner has effectively already fulfilled his obligation.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Ami, what actually happened to Rabbi Tarfon's ruling that 'the priest chooses the better of the two' lambs?
o: It was never actually his opinion
He retracted it and instead holds that the priest and owner always divide the value of the remaining lamb
It was upheld unanimously by later authorities
It only applied to female offspring
quiz.e: Rabbi Ami reports that Rabbi Tarfon retracted his original ruling; the mishna's text preserving 'the priest chooses the better one' simply was never updated to reflect his final position of dividing the value.
